extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and philosophers of science studying methods of induction and deduction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and applying modes of investigation (deductive, empirical/experimental, and simple observation) for phenomena arising from many concurrent causes, and on how to establish laws of causes and deduce combined effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of Causes undermines simple observation (Method of Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect arises from the union of many causes, instances of the effect will not reliably agree in the presence (or absence) of any single cause; hence mere collation of instances (simple observation / Method of Agreement) is inapplicable to ascertain the conditions of such effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Recovery from disease depends on many influences; even if mercury tends to cure, there will be abundant recoveries without mercury and failures with mercury. At best simple observation can yield only a vague general impression unless confirmed by other methods; multiplied accurate returns might show slight differences but are of very secondary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/Experimental Method must be purely empirical when applied to complex cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical method operates by trying different combinations of causes directly on the complex case (experiments upon the complex phenomenon itself) and must be kept free from deductive elements if judged purely empirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experiments on simpler cases are used and then reasoned from to the complex case, that is deduction, not pure empirical method. To judge the empirical method fairly, exclude prior knowledge of simpler laws and aim experiments directly at the specific question (e.g., 'Does mercury tend to cure the particular disease?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions for valid experimentation (control/avoid confounding causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When devising an experiment to ascertain an agent's effect, one must introduce the agent into circumstances exactly ascertained and exclude or account for any other causes whose effects might be confounded with those of the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If other influencing circumstances are present (known or unknown) they disguise the agent's effect and preclude knowing whether it has produced the observed result. If forced to admit other causes, make them such that their influence can be computed and allowed for so the agent's residual effect is apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference is unavailing when other causes operate during the transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing the same case at two times (before/after an experiment) fails for complex phenomena if other causes have been operating during the transition, because those other causes may have produced the observed change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also, comparing different cases (supposedly identical except for one factor) is chimerical for complicated phenomena because two cases similar in all respects but one rarely occur and cannot be known to be exactly similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method on complex conjunct effects can at best show frequent association
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific experiments on complex cases typically cannot definitively establish that a cause produces an effect; at best they can show that a cause is often followed by a certain effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the share of any single cause in a conjunct effect is usually small and may be thwarted by other tendencies, experiments will often only indicate a tendency rather than decisive causal determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive (a priori) method appropriate when direct methods fail
rubrics_metrics.description: When observation and experiment are inefficient (as with phenomena from many combined causes), the deductive method — computing effects from the laws of the separate causes — remains the main source of knowledge about conditions and recurrence of complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deductive method treats the whole assemblage as a balance of tendencies and requires knowing the laws of the individual causes to compute their combined effect; the method is intellectual and often necessary for social, political, or other highly composite phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method consists of induction, ratiocination, verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductive method comprises three operations: (1) a direct inductive operation to furnish premisses, (2) ratiocination (reasoning/calculation) from those premisses, and (3) verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a prior deduction substitutes for induction in particular cases, the ultimate premisses must be grounded in induction (observation/experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: First requisite for deduction: ascertain laws of each separate cause
rubrics_metrics.description: To deduce the law of an effect from the laws of the tendencies that produce it, the first requisite is knowledge of the law of each concurrent cause, obtained by prior observation, experiment, or deduction ultimately grounded in induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This often requires studying each cause separately, or at least in combinations where other agencies' effects can be calculated and allowed for. In social phenomena, the causes are human actions and external circumstances; in physiology, mechanical/chemical/vital laws of tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study laws of tendencies in cases where they operate alone where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a tendency is best discovered from instances in which that tendency operates uncombined or combined only with causes whose effects can be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is difficult or impossible to derive the law of a tendency from instances where it is counteracted or heavily modified by other causes; e.g., laws of motion could not be found from bodies kept at rest by equilibrium of opposing forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pathological facts as natural experiments in physiology
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological conditions often present a definite local disturbance approximating an experiment, allowing the investigator to observe effects of a disturbance in one organ or function with others initially unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is valuable only when early stages are observed (before secondary effects spread) and when one can determine the disturbance was local (not constitutional); otherwise cause/effect ordering among derangements is indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: For discovering general laws prefer experiments in health rather than disease
rubrics_metrics.description: When experiments aim to discover general laws (not to solve a particular practical question), the best cases are those whose circumstances can be most accurately ascertained — generally the healthy state rather than disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In health, physiological phenomena are comparatively fixed and the introduced disturbing cause is more likely to have observable effects that can be attributed to it rather than to unpredictable agencies present during disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations is useful but encumbered in complex subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of concomitant variations can provide resources for ascertaining laws of causes when separation is impossible, but it is encumbered by the peculiar difficulties of subjects like physiology or social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with concomitant variations, identifying causation vs. collateral correlation remains uncertain; results may be empirical uniformities with unclear causal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and historical phenomena resist experimental/inductive approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: In politics and history plurality of causes is extreme, influences are numerous and perpetually changing, and artificial experiments are usually impossible or vitiated by temporal changes; thus direct inductive/experimental methods are largely inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodies of experimental reasoning in political argument (e.g., 'an institution cannot be bad because a country prospered under it') ignore plurality of causes. Introducing a law or measure into national affairs takes time to reveal effects and concurrent changes will confound induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination (calculation) from known laws yields expected effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the laws of the causes have been ascertained, the next stage is to determine what effect a given combination of those causes will produce by ratiocination — often involving numerical and geometrical calculation when precision permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High mathematical theorems may be required for precise computation (e.g., celestial mechanics); where precision is impossible or unnecessary, ratiocination still means reasoning from a general law to particular cases to predict effects or infer antecedent conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction can answer two complementary questions
rubrics_metrics.description: By ratiocination from the separate laws of causes one may (a) determine the effect expected from a certain combination of causes, and (b) determine what combination of causes would produce a given effect (i.e., antecedent conditions of recurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires sufficient knowledge of the particular circumstances of the case to apply the general laws; without adequate premisses from induction, such deductions lack reliability.
